names.name: Brahman (in its primary sense only Viṣṇu)

descriptions: the one independent reality; everything else is dependent on him (Tattvasaṅkhyāna 1)
free of all defects and full of all good qualities, each unlimited (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya, maṅgala)
known through the true scriptures alone, not by bare reasoning or the senses (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1)
source of the creation, maintenance, dissolution, control, knowledge, ignorance, bondage and release of the world (BSB 1.1.2)
of the nature of full bliss, knowledge and power; the fourfold Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, Turīya in all beings (Māṇḍūkya-bhāṣya)
his qualities, acts, forms and avatāras are identical with him; there is no internal difference in him (MBTN 1.69; VTN 3)
the primary meaning of every word and letter and the great purport of all scripture (BSB 1.1.1; VTN 1)
beyond the perishable (all souls) and the imperishable (Lakṣmī) (VTN 2)
negations: not without qualities — 'nirguṇa' means free of prakṛti's qualities (Karmanirṇaya)
not identical with the soul or the world; not their material cause
not subject to any defect, even in his descents (VTN 3)
not an attributeless consciousness — such a Brahman would be the Mādhyamika's void (Anuvyākhyāna 2.2.241–242)
relation_to_self: Eternally different from every soul; the soul is his reflection (pratibimba), wholly dependent on him, moved by him within, and in liberation enjoys its own bliss in his presence, desiring only in accord with his will and still graded and distinct.
relation_to_world: The world is real, eternally different from him and wholly dependent; he is its efficient cause and controller, prakṛti its material cause; he brings about its creation, maintenance, dissolution, bondage and release.
caveat: Dvaita affirms one supreme, independent reality and can read Ṛgveda 1.164.46 as 'the wise call the one (Viṣṇu) by many names', since for Madhva all names primarily denote Viṣṇu. It rejects any reading of 'one truth' as an identity in which souls, world and God are ultimately one; it rejects treating difference as provisional, empirical (vyāvahārika) or merely a standpoint; and it rejects placing other deities (Brahmā, Śiva and the rest, who are dependent souls) on a par with Viṣṇu as equal names of the supreme. Any reconciliation that dissolves the five differences is one the tradition explicitly refuses.

descriptions: The Uttarādi Maṭha holds the Dvaita teaching on the ultimate without variation; see ult:dvaita.
caveat: As in ult:dvaita; the maṭha has no separate doctrine of the ultimate.
